artworks.title: Ulysses and His Dog
artworks.description: Flaxman's outline engraving for the Odyssey freezes the recognition: Argos lifts his head from the dung-heap as the disguised Odysseus passes — the twenty-year wait ended in a single glance.

artworks.title: The Dog of Ulysses
artworks.description: Ingres isolates Argos as a study of loyalty: the hound of Ithaca, neglected yet still knowing — Odyssey 17 distilled into a single animal portrait.

artworks.title: Odysseus Recognized by His Dog Argos
artworks.description: A Rijksmuseum plate from an Odysseus cycle shows the beggar-king and the dying dog — Argos as the only creature on Ithaca who sees through the disguise before he dies.

artworks.title: Odysseus and Argos
artworks.description: Barre's print returns to the same Homeric instant: Argos knows his master at the threshold of the palace — fidelity staged as the quietest recognition in the epic.

popCulture.title: Odyssey
popCulture.creator: Homer
popCulture.description: Book 17 gives Argos his entire life in a few dozen lines: bred by Odysseus, left on the dung-heap, knowing his master at a glance, and dying as the king enters the hall — the epic's most concentrated image of loyalty.

popCulture.title: Argos (dog)
popCulture.description: Odysseus' hound — the dog who waited twenty years and recognized the beggar at the gate before his strength failed.
